subject: Post-call: clarifying streaming QPS / tokens/sec & peak concurrency
messages:
From: Olga Petrov <olga_petrov@redwood.ai>
To: Ethan Wu <ethan.wu@acme.com>, Priya Sinha <priya@acme.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>, Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>
Date: Wed, 21 Apr 2027 15:10:00 -0700
Subject: Post-call: clarifying streaming QPS / tokens/sec & peak concurrency

Hi Ethan / Priya — thanks again for the call today. Quick recap and a few clarifying asks so we can size a canary and draft a mutual action plan: 

Call summary (high level)
- Use case: payment fraud investigation assistant embedded in Acme’s merchant portal. Low-latency streaming responses to agents during case triage.
- Primary SLOs: p95 latency target for first token <= 350ms (goal 250ms), steady-state per-agent throughput target ~6 QPS, peak burst up to 180 concurrent streaming sessions across region.
- Typical prompt size: 220–320 tokens inbound, average response length ~420 tokens (streamed).

Numbers you confirmed on the call (please correct if I transcribed incorrectly):
- Average QPS per active agent session: 6 QPS (request/second)
- Average tokens per response: 420 tokens (streaming)
- Expected active sessions during business hours: 1,200 steady-state, with peak events up to 3,600 (3x) for short windows
- Concurrent streaming connections to support during peak: 360–540 (they mentioned 180 per region; want to validate multi-region routing)

Sizing ask for Redwood to validate:
- Steady tokens/sec = steady_active_sessions * QPS * avg_tokens_per_response. With 1,200 steady-state sessions: 1,200 * 6 * 420 = 3,024,000 tokens/sec (please confirm you expect that math to hold for your workload).
- Peak tokens/sec (3x peak multiplier) ≈ 9,072,000 tokens/sec (short bursts).
- Long-tail concurrency: we need to know how long streaming connections remain idle between agent interactions (affects connection count and KV cache TTL).

Operational questions:
1) Do you expect true server-initiated streaming (server pushes tokens continuously) or will clients request and then keep the socket idle between chunks?
2) Typical chunk size per flush (tokens) and flush frequency (ms) — this impacts our batching and latency path.
3) Are there heavy-output cases (>= 1,200 tokens) we should guard for with model truncation / stop tokens?

Attachments: I attached the draft Mutual Action Plan and a quick snapshot CSV of the numbers you shared; see attached.

Next steps (proposed):
- Ethan / Priya: confirm the three sizing numbers above and the idle-connection TTL assumption.
- Redwood: provision a 2-week canary config that mirrors your peak/multipliers; recommend enabling KV prefix cache + streaming-optimized scheduling for canary.
- Schedule a 30m follow-up next week to review canary telemetry and confirm rollout criteria.

Thanks — I’ll hold off on final canary config until you confirm the numbers.

— Olga
Olga Petrov | Senior AE, Redwood Inference
olga_petrov@redwood.ai | +1 (415) 555-0183
Redwood Inference

From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
To: Olga Petrov <olga_petrov@redwood.ai>, Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>
Cc: Ethan Wu <ethan.wu@acme.com>
Date: Thu, 22 Apr 2027 09:05:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Post-call: clarifying streaming QPS / tokens/sec & peak concurrency

Thanks Olga — a couple of clarifications from infra/ops perspective before we finalize the canary sizing: 

1) The tokens/sec math looks correct if their definition of QPS maps to full request round-trips per second per active agent. We should confirm whether their reported QPS is "input requests" or "streamed-chunk flushes". If it's the latter, the tokens/sec is much lower.

2) Streaming concurrency vs HTTP connection concurrency: do they plan to keep an open SSE/WebSocket per agent? If they multiplex multiple requests over one connection (unlikely for UI agent flows), our concurrency needs drop.

3) KV cache TTL: we recommend 60s for agent-case reuse; if clients keep many idle sockets open for minutes, memory demands and eviction behavior change. Can Ethan confirm average idle time between agent prompts?

4) Backpressure plan: for peak bursts, do they want graceful degradation (downgrade to smaller model/quantized shard) or queuing with a 200–500ms added tail latency? Need customer preference to design fallback policy.

Action: Aditya / Karthik — can you draft two canary configs:
A) Latency-first: p95-first-token <= 250ms, prefer smaller batch sizes, reserved nv12 slices for priority traffic
B) Cost-first: allow p95-first-token <= 350ms, higher batching, enable fractional quantization profile

I'll stitch config diffs and share with EPA for approval.

— Marissa
Marissa Cole | Performance Lead, Redwood Inference
marissa_cole@redwood.ai

On Thu, Apr 22, 2027 at 11:15 AM, Ethan Wu <ethan.wu@acme.com> wrote:
> Thanks all — replying inline to confirm a few items.
> 
> On 4/21/27, Olga Petrov <olga_petrov@redwood.ai> wrote:
> > With 1,200 steady-state sessions: 1,200 * 6 * 420 = 3,024,000 tokens/sec (please confirm that math)
> 
> That math is correct based on how we count QPS (requests that kick off a streamed response). A couple of clarifications:
> - Our front-end keeps a single WebSocket per agent tab. Each agent tab directly correlates to an active session.
> - Idle time between agent prompts is typically 45–90s during normal hours; during after-hours it can be many minutes.
> - Peak events: the 3,600 peak sessions number is an extreme sale day; more realistic traffic surges are 1.8–2.5x for 5–20 minute windows.
> - Chunking: we currently flush ~40–80 tokens per chunk, every 80–140ms on average.
> - Heavy outputs: rare (<<1% of requests), but we do have occasional long transcripts up to 2,400 tokens.
> 
> For fallbacks we'd prefer graceful degradation (smaller model variant) over queuing; customers value responsiveness over truncated content.
> 
> We'll confirm final numbers by EOD tomorrow.
> 
> — Ethan

From: Ethan Wu <ethan.wu@acme.com>
To: Olga Petrov <olga_petrov@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>, Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.ai>
Cc: Priya Sinha <priya@acme.com>
Date: Fri, 23 Apr 2027 11:20:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Post-call: clarifying streaming QPS / tokens/sec & peak concurrency

Olga / team — confirming the items Marissa called out. Apologies for the earlier rough numbers; here's a concise statement of intent so you can size: 

- Steady-state active sessions: 1,100–1,300 (we'll use 1,200 as a midpoint)
- QPS per active session: 5–7 (use 6 as median)
- Avg response tokens (streamed): 400–440 (use 420)
- Typical chunk flush: 50–70 tokens every ~100ms
- Idle socket median: 60s
- Peak multiplier for canary sizing: 2.5x sustained for 10–20 minutes; extreme events may briefly hit 3x
- Preference: graceful fallback to smaller model variant rather than queueing; prefer transparency in which model variant served.

I'll upload a short CSV with sampled minute-level telemetry tomorrow morning (attached in my follow-up).

Thanks — Ethan
Ethan Wu | Platform PM, Acme Payments
ethan.wu@acme.com

From: Olga Petrov <olga_petrov@redwood.ai>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>, Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.ai>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>, Ethan Wu <ethan.wu@acme.com>
Date: Sun, 25 Apr 2027 08:30:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Post-call: clarifying streaming QPS / tokens/sec & peak concurrency

Thanks Ethan — that is super helpful. Final notes and next steps below: 

1) Canary config: we'll provision two canaries this week (Latency-first + Cost-first per Marissa's note). Target region: us-west-2; we'll mirror your multi-region routing for later stages.

2) KV cache TTL: default 60s for canary; if we see >120s median idle we will raise to 180s to improve hit rates.

3) Streaming tune: we'll set chunk target to 60 tokens / 100ms for canary to align with your flush pattern. That should keep p95-first-token <= 300ms on latency-first canary.

4) Fallback policy: implement automatic model-variant fallback with explicit header on response so you can surface which model variant served. We'll expose that in the canary telemetry dashboard.

5) Telemetry + rollout: once canary is running we'll capture minute-level tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99-first-token latency, connection counts, and model-variant percentages. We'll schedule a 30m review on Fri 2027-04-30 10:00 PT.

6) Action items: Ethan — upload the CSV sample and confirm whether the 2.5x peak multiplier (our working canary) is acceptable.

I'll create the HubSpot activity and DocuSign expectations doc and loop legal once the canary meets p95 targets.

— Olga
